name: Great Wagon Road
other_names: Great Philadelphia Wagon Road; Great Valley Road
year_note: Built up in stages from the 1730s to 1760s; no single opening year. Philadelphia–Lancaster King's Road 1733; Lexington VA routing 1745 (secondary)
via: Lancaster; York; Shenandoah Valley; Salisbury NC; Charlotte NC; Camden or Ninety Six SC
native_path_basis: Described as originally a Native hunting, trade and war trail (Great Minquas / Conestoga Path)
unverified_note: Opening dates by segment not confirmed; encyclopedia pages read only through search summaries (NCpedia returned 403)
source: South Carolina Encyclopedia n.d.; NCpedia n.d.

name: Forbes Road
year_note: Cut as a military road in 1758; settler route after 1763. Upgrade as Pennsylvania State Road 1791 rests on one source
unverified_note: 1791 state-road date unverified (single source); Hulbert not opened in this pass (Gutenberg unavailable)

name: Braddock's Road
year_note: Cut in 1755; stopped short of Fort Duquesne after Braddock's defeat
native_path_basis: Washington's 1754 road (its predecessor) followed the Nemacolin Trail (Armao)
unverified_note: Only encyclopedic summaries seen; endpoints and later use need a primary or NPS source

name: Crown Point Road
year_note: Cut 1759, widened for wagons 1760; described as the New England settler route into Vermont after 1763
unverified_note: Post-1763 settler use is a general statement only

name: Wilderness Road
year_note: Blazed 1775 (Boone for Henderson's Transylvania Co.); Virginia road act 1779; wagon road 1795 (Speed, quoted by Armao) or 1796 (NPS, FHWA)
endpoint_a: Long Island of the Holston (Kingsport TN)
via: Cumberland Gap; Martin's Station; Dix River fork
native_path_basis: "a constellation of worn Indian footpaths and buffalo trails" (Armao)
unverified_note: Wagon-road year 1795 vs 1796; Long Island of the Holston start from secondary summaries only
source: Longfellow n.d.; Armao n.d.; NPS n.d.

name: Avery's Trace
other_names: Old North Carolina Road; Emery Road
year_note: NC road act 1787; by 1788 still a rough trail marked by blazed trees
endpoint_a: South end of Clinch Mountain (East TN)
via: Clinch River near Oak Ridge; Winter's Gap; Emory River near Wartburg
native_path_basis: Northern route followed sections of Tollunteeskee's Trail

name: Walton Road
year_note: 1795 act for a wagon road Knoxville–Nashville; made a turnpike 1801; 'broad and commodious' by 1802

name: Philadelphia and Lancaster Turnpike
year_note: Construction start given as 1792 or 1793; opened 1795. First long-distance stone-and-gravel road built to formal plans (FHWA)
unverified_note: Construction start year disputed (1792 vs 1793)

name: Great Genesee Road
year_note: State act 22 Mar 1794 (Old Fort Schuyler to Genesee River); $2,200 for improving it 1797; Utica–Geneva stage 1797; extension to Buffalo by law 1798 (secondary)
native_path_basis: Williamson called it "little better than an Indian trail" (secondary quote)
nations_on_route_as_named: Oneida; Onondaga; Cayuga; Seneca (Haudenosaunee lands; see R1)
unverified_note: Act date, stage date and 1798 extension seen only in search summaries of county histories; Greene 1925 confirms the 1797 $2,200

name: Mohawk Turnpike
year_note: Incorporated 1800 and work began; opening year not found
unverified_note: Opening year blank

name: Seneca Road
year_note: Chartered 1800 running west from Utica; took over the Utica–Canandaigua section of the Genesee Road (secondary)
unverified_note: Western endpoint and opening year from secondary sources only

name: Great Western Turnpike
year_note: First Great Western Turnpike incorporated 1799 (one list gives 15 Mar 1799; a county history gives 1798 for construction); Second Great Western 1801
unverified_note: 1798 vs 1799; opening year not found
source: Greene 1925; New York State Library n.d.

name: Zane's Trace
year_note: Act of 17 May 1796; work began summer 1796; built 1796–97 (opening 1797 per a Lancaster OH marker); wagon road only after Ohio's 1804 appropriation
endpoint_b: Limestone (Maysville) KY (Ohio River crossing at Aberdeen OH)
native_path_basis: Kept to high ground 'after the manner of Indian trails'; may have followed the old Mingo Trail in places (FHWA, citing Stewart)
unverified_note: Opening year from a marker; FHWA gives no completion date

name: Natchez Trace
year_note: Congress set up the Nashville–Natchez post route 1800; Choctaw and Chickasaw agreed 1801 that the US may open the road; US troops opened it 1801–02; first improvement appropriation 1806; steamboat became the usual travel mode 1820–30
native_path_basis: Earlier Native path (first recorded trip 1730 per NPS)
source: NPS n.d. (Chronology of the Natchez Trace)

name: Federal Road (Creek Nation)
year_note: Route surveyed 1804, approved by Congress Mar 1805; Creek treaty 14 Nov 1805; postal road funded Apr 1806 (contract 15 Aug 1806); widened to a 16-ft military road, opened Nov 1811
endpoint_a: Athens GA (1806 postal route); Milledgeville GA (1811 road)
endpoint_b: Fort Stoddert AL (on to New Orleans)
via: Fort Mitchell; Chattahoochee River near Columbus GA
native_path_basis: Before the road, travellers used 'a series of Indian routes' (Harrell)
unverified_note: Hawkins counted 3,726 westward travellers at the Flint River agency Oct 1811–Mar 1812

name: Unicoi Turnpike
year_note: Company of Tennessee, Georgia and Cherokee members formed 1813 (a Georgia marker says chartered 1812); finished c. 1817 (marker) or open as toll road by 1819
unverified_note: Charter 1812 vs 1813; opening c. 1817 vs 1819; southern endpoint varies. Later the first leg of removal for over 3,000 Cherokee (belongs to L5)

name: National Road
year_note: Authorized 1806; construction began 1811; reached Wheeling 1818. Columbus 1833 or 1834; federal work ended at Vandalia IL c. 1839 (sources disagree)
unverified_note: Columbus (1833 vs 1834) and Vandalia (c. 1839) dates unverified
source: FHWA n.d. (Maryland's Bank Road); FHWA n.d. (National Road fact sheet)

name: Jackson's Military Road
year_note: Funded 1816; survey 1817; Army work began May 1817; reported open May 1820
endpoint_b: Madisonville LA (Lake Pontchartrain; toward New Orleans)
nations_on_route_as_named: Chickasaw; Choctaw (lands crossed; not stated in sources read)
unverified_note: Length 516 mi (EoA) vs 436 mi; start 1816 vs 1817

name: Chicago Road
year_note: Federal funds and survey 1825; built 1829–36 (Michigan marker); a 'rudimentary road' by 1827 per another source
unverified_note: Completion date disputed (1827 / 1831 / 1836)

name: Ohio River (flatboat route)
year_note: In use throughout; 1785 first American cargo reaches Natchez via the Ohio and Mississippi; first steamboat from Pittsburgh reaches Natchez 1811
unverified_note: No opening year by design; endpoints general
source: NPS n.d. (Chronology of the Natchez Trace)

name: Erie Canal
year_note: Construction began 4 Jul 1817 (groundbreaking at Rome per Britannica); opened 26 Oct 1825
unverified_note: Cross-check against Atack GIS (L6 source)

name: Ohio and Erie Canal
year_note: Begun 1825; completed 1832 (308 mi)
unverified_note: Cross-check against Atack GIS

name: Main Line of Public Works
year_note: Authorized 1826; Philadelphia–Columbia section opened Sep 1832; main system complete 1834
unverified_note: Cross-check against Atack GIS
